title: Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978)
summary: The plaintiff’s direct claim against the nondiverse third-party defendant could not rest on the original diversity action.
notes:
Section 1367(b) later expressly addresses specified claims by plaintiffs in cases founded solely on diversity. Analyze its text rather than treating every later-added claim as automatically excluded.

James Kroger was electrocuted when a crane boom came near a high-tension line in Iowa; his widow sued the Omaha Public Power District (a Nebraska corporation) in diversity, OPPD impleaded Owen under Rule 14, Kroger amended to sue Owen directly, OPPD won summary judgment, and Owen's Iowa principal place of business surfaced only at trial.

Procedurally, the jury returned a verdict for Kroger, the Eighth Circuit affirmed, and the Supreme Court reversed in an opinion by Justice Stewart; Justice White, joined by Justice Brennan, dissented, arguing ancillary jurisdiction should reach the claim because the plaintiff had not tried to evade complete diversity.

Congress codified the Kroger result in 28 U.S.C. § 1367(b), which withholds supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases over claims by plaintiffs against persons made parties under Rules 14, 19, 20 or 24 when that would be inconsistent with § 1332.

sections.Parties: Kroger, an Iowa plaintiff, sued Omaha Public Power District, which brought Owen Equipment into the case. Kroger then asserted her own claim against Owen.
sections.Material Facts: The wrongful-death action began with diverse parties. Owen appeared to be a Nebraska corporation for the relevant purposes, but the record later established that its principal place of business was Iowa. Kroger and Owen therefore shared Iowa citizenship. The claim against the original defendant no longer supplied a way around that problem merely because Owen had entered through third-party procedure.
sections.Procedural History: After litigation proceeded against Owen, the citizenship problem surfaced. The Supreme Court held that the plaintiff’s direct claim lacked the necessary jurisdictional basis.
sections.Issue: Could a diversity plaintiff assert a direct claim against a nondiverse third-party defendant solely because the original defendant had impleaded it?
sections.Holding: No. The plaintiff could not circumvent complete diversity by using the third-party route to reach a party she could not originally have sued in diversity.
sections.Reasoning: The Court distinguished defensive claims introduced by a defendant from an affirmative choice by the plaintiff to seek relief against another party. Factual relationship and convenience did not justify ignoring the restrictions of the original diversity grant. The problem concerns the jurisdictional basis of a particular claim between particular parties, not simply whether the third-party defendant is already physically present in the litigation.

learning.why: The plaintiff’s direct claim against the nondiverse third-party defendant could not rest on the original diversity action.

topics.cp-supplemental-diversity: The plaintiff could not use a defendant’s impleader to assert a direct claim against a nondiverse party.
topics.cp-impleader: Jurisdiction over a third-party claim does not automatically extend to the plaintiff’s separate claim against that third party.
topics.cp-citizenship: The actual principal place of business, rather than an assumed corporate address, affected diversity.
topics.cp-usc-1367: Section 1367(b) codifies Kroger by denying supplemental jurisdiction in diversity cases over plaintiffs' claims against parties joined under Rules 14, 19, 20 or 24.
topics.cp-supplemental-history: Kroger is the leading pre-1990 ancillary-jurisdiction decision and explains why § 1367 was written as it was.
topics.cp-frcp-14: Owen entered the case as a Rule 14 third-party defendant, and the case turns on the difference between the defendant's impleader claim and the plaintiff's later direct claim.
